Marco Polo Marine sounds profit warning
article:
In a bourse filing on Nov 20, Mainboard-listed Marco Polo Marine (MPM) has warned of a drop in earnings for FY2026 ended Sept 30.

The anticipated lower earnings are due to the absence of the one-off gain arising from the disposal of its shareholding interest in its joint venture company, Marco Polo Offshore (IV) Pte Ltd, which was recognised in FY2025; and (a significantly lower reversal of impairment losses on certain vessels in FY2026 as compared to FY2025.

The filing adds that more details will be disclosed when the company announces its unaudited financial results for FY2026 on or before Nov 29, 2026.

Earlier this year, MPM announced the spin-off of its shipyard business via a reverse takeover of Fuji Offset Plates Manufacturing in a deal worth up to $139 million. Its subsidiary, PKR Offshore, had also planned to submit its application to be listed on the Taiwan stock exchange by the third quarter of this year, but no public announcement has been made on the status of submission.

This year also saw offshore & marine and hotel magnate Michael Kum acquire 225 million shares in the counter via married deals.

Ytd, shares in Marco Polo Marine have dropped 44%, closing at 9.5 cents on Nov 20.

title: Uni-Asia to pay dividends of not less than 25% of patmi as policy
article:
Shipping and property firm Uni-Asia Group has announced a formal dividend policy in its 3QFY2026 business update. The Mainboard-listed company will pay a minimum of 25% of annual patmi in dividends from FY2026 onwards.

The announcement comes as SGX RegCo mandated Mainboard and Catalist issuers under Rule 710C to maintain a formal dividend policy and describe it in their annual reports.

Besides the dividend announcement, Uni-Asia announced the Nov 17 sale completion of dry-bulk carrier MV Ansac Pride for around US$15 million in cash, with the firm booking a gain of about US$5 million.

The vessel sale is part of fleet renewal and proceeds will fund the company’s newbuild programme. Uni-Asia adds that the vessel was sold at its target price and repays vessel-level bank debt.

In 2026, Uni-Asia placed orders for two newbuilds, which are scheduled for completion in 2028 and 2029/2030. It has also increased its stake in the Uni Harmony from 18% to 55.6%, gaining majority control by paying around US$5 million, which is under a quarter of the US$20.53 million valuation.

Besides gaining majority control for a bargain while limiting cash outlay, the purchase also enables Uni-Asia to consolidate recurring charter income and cashflow.

See also: HG Metal’s 2HFY2026 net profit down 30% y-o-y to $4.1 mil, declares final dividend of 2 cents

On chartering performance, the average day rate has increased nearly 17% y-o-y for 9MFY2026 ended Sept 30. The number of hire days also increased 35% to 2,336, reflecting strong overall demand.

Looking ahead, Uni-Asia expects “firm” earnings for the shipping segment into 2027, supported by demand outstripping supply as shipping scrapping outpaces newbuilds entering the market. With Uni-Asia’s younger fleet profile, it also stands to benefit as the European Union’s emissions trading scheme is phased in, as older ships and more fuel-inefficient ships incur higher operational costs due to carbon taxes.

See also: Seatrium’s net orderbook drops to $12.2 bil as it says order win momentum strengthening with recent contracts

In addition to its shipping interests, Uni-Asia is also a property player in the Japanese market. In past years, it has been diversifying from a build-and-sell model into property management to generate recurring income.

For 9MFY2026, it completed six ALERO projects, with seven under development. ALERO projects comprise the conversion of old Tokyo sites into modern residential buildings that can be sold or rented out. Uni-Asia has made the decision to retain selected projects for rental to generate recurring revenue and reduce reliance on one-off sales.

Its subsidiary Uni-Asia Capital also manages assets across public infrastructure, healthcare, residential and hospitality, generating recurring income. However, AUM dipped to JPY68.7 billion as at Sept 30 from end-June’s JPY70.5 billion.

Shares in Uni-Asia closed unchanged on Nov 20 at 92 cents.

title: Bitcoin extends reversal from Trump election gain to hit below US$56,000
article:
(Nov 21): Bitcoin fell to the lowest level in over two years, extending its reversal from market darling after the re-election of US President Donald Trump to a casualty of a broader retreat from speculative bets.

The original cryptocurrency slumped 6% in the US on Friday and another 5.7% in Asia on Saturday to US$55,533, its weakest since September 2024. It has lost more than half its value since reaching a peak above US$126,000 in October 2025 and is now worth less than it was when crypto-friendly Trump retook the White House.

Bitcoin has been caught in a confluence of pressures in recent weeks. A hack of Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, at the end of October rattled digital assets, while sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections the following week fuelled concerns that the crypto industry’s push for friendlier rules has lost momentum.

“The broader market has shifted into a sharp lack of confidence, and investors are de-risking,” said Andy Baehr, the managing director of asset management at GSR. “Bitcoin is along for the ride here, typically weak in deleveraging environments.”

The latest leg lower has been fuelled by investors pulling money from bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) amid an unraveling of the artificial-intelligence (AI) trade. Bitcoin ETFs have seen year-to-date outflows of more than US$3 billion ($3.9 billion).

The broader backdrop is becoming less favourable as well. For much of the past decade, cryptocurrencies occupied a privileged place in the risk-taking economy. Now a stronger dollar and rising expectations of another US Federal Reserve (Fed) rate increase are adding to the pressure.

See also: Bitcoin options traders brace for slide to US$60,000 after selloff

The market is pricing a more aggressive Fed rate hike and a slowdown in the AI buildout, prompting “an excessively negative market interpretation right now”, said Fabian Dori, the chief investment officer of Sygnum Bank.

On Friday, bitcoin’s slide triggered the liquidation of roughly US$2 billion in long crypto bets over 24 hours, with bitcoin positions accounting for the majority of that sum, according to Coinglass data.

“What made the move so fast was leverage,” said Andrew Yang, a research analyst at Kaiko. “As Nasdaq losses deepened again in late-morning New York trading, bitcoin broke below US$60,000, triggering US$94.6 million in BTC liquidations on Binance, Bybit and OKX in a single hour.”

See also: Bitcoin slides below US$70,000 as inflation concerns hurt crypto

The downturn is unfolding at what should have been a triumphant moment for the industry.

With Trump as the US president, crypto has secured many of the victories it spent the better part of a decade pursuing: a sympathetic White House, friendlier regulators, institutional acceptance and a legislative framework that increasingly treats digital assets as a permanent part of the financial system. Yet rather than unleashing a new wave of demand, those milestones have coincided with one of bitcoin’s deepest retreats in years.

Earlier crypto crashes were punctuated by spectacular failures or waves of forced selling. This downturn has been marked by a steadier erosion in demand. Bitcoin fell even as inflation worries mounted, doing little to bolster its case as a hedge. And when geopolitical turmoil sent investors looking for safety, they turned to traditional havens.

Institutional acceptance hasn’t gone away, but the early enthusiasm has cooled. The question now is whether the biggest buyers will keep adding to their holdings at the pace the industry once expected.

title: Anthropic slides 8.5% to shrink IPO gain as AI trade unravels
article:
(Nov 21): Anthropic PBC shares erased a portion of their first-day jump on Friday, testing investors’ faith after the artificial intelligence (AI) lab delivered the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history.

Shares in the company behind the Claude chatbot plunged almost to the IPO price, before paring the loss. The stock settled at US$88.91 each, down 8.5% from the end of their debut on Thursday. The trading gives Anthropic a market value of about US$1.6 trillion ($2.1 trillion), ranking it among the 15 biggest publicly traded companies in the world.

The drop came at the same time as the so-called over-allotment option, also known as a greenshoe, was exercised, allowing the underwriting banks to sell additional shares. The over-allotment lifted the total raised by Anthropic and the co-founders selling shares in the offering to US$119.5 billion, with US$93.5 billion in the IPO and US$26 billion from the concurrent private placement.

“There’s a buyers’ strike for Anthropic as well as the wider AI and tech trade,” according to Emmanuel Valavanis of Forte Securities.

“There are many clients who appear to have been left without allocations and, having been left out of the party, aren’t prepared to pick up the pieces from the hangover. With no skin in the game, and no index considerations for risk of relative performance, investors can sit on the sidelines and wait for longer term price discovery rather than risk getting caught out,” Valavanis said.

See also: AI’s billions and slick pledges heap pressure on pharma veterans

Stocks were roiled by a sell-off that spread from Asia to the US, with the Nasdaq 100 Index falling 5.6% and the S&P 500 Index sinking 3.7%.

Anthropic’s IPO made history not only because of its size, but also because the company is the first frontier AI model maker to go public. The trading represents a test of whether investors have appetite for companies pioneering the technology itself, rather than the tools to develop it such as chips and data centres. It also sets up a debut for rival OpenAI, which isn’t planning to go public before 2027.

The IPO delivered outsize returns to its backers and pushing up the combined wealth of its seven founders to US$166 billion. The fundraise eclipsed the record set in June by SpaceX’s IPO, which ultimately totalled US$86.2 billion. Goldman Sachs Group Inc, Morgan Stanley and 20 other banks earned a record US$550 million in fees for their work on Anthropic’s IPO.

See also: AI investors have overlooked obvious risks

“We are impressed by the wealth creation this company is generating, in a matter of a few years and with reasonable free cash flow burn,” said Raphael Thuin, the head of capital markets strategies at Tikehau Capital.

“To get exposed to AI though, we tend to favour more diversified businesses, and in any case we would like to see the post IPO volatility fade before engaging further.”

Anthropic won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualised from a shorter period — to US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings showed.

Claude Code, the company’s coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by Nasa engineers, the filing showed. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering US$100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.

Investors considering taking stakes may decide to wait out the market turmoil first. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, spiked to more than 29 on Friday morning, well above the level where companies typically consider the market welcoming to IPOs.

“We would look at buying in the open market if the stock get close or even below the IPO price,” said Olivier David, a fund manager at Vega IS.

Anthropic’s listing joins companies linked to AI that have pushed US IPO volume to an all-time high. Including Anthropic, first time stock sales raised US$258 billion this year, beating 2021’s US$195 billion haul, excluding financial vehicles such as blank-cheque firms, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.

“What we saw yesterday (Thursday) was real excitement around a big deal getting done,” said Ann Miletti, the head of equity investments at Allspring Global Investments. “That demand is a positive. It doesn’t take away the fear or the worry that we don’t know what we don’t know about AI, and the biggest question in investors’ minds is what are the returns?”
